1000600.etyen:
From elfenben + -s- + kysten, literally “the ivory coast”. The alternative spelling Elfenbeinskysten instead contains the synonymous Bokmål form elfenbein (“ivory”).
The name belongs to a historical European naming tradition in which stretches of the West African coast were named after important commodities traded there. It refers to the historical trade in ivory along this part of the coast. Compare Portuguese Costa do Marfim (“Ivory Coast”) and French Côte d'Ivoire (“Ivory Coast”). The precise language from which the Norwegian formation was immediately modelled is uncertain.

1001112.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Jakob, from Latin Iacobus, from Ancient Greek Ἰακώβ (Iakṓb), from Hebrew יַעֲקֹב (Yaʿăqōḇ). The meaning is disputed: the Old Testament associates the name with “holding the heel”, while another interpretation is “may God protect”. The name is First attested in the 12th century in Norway.
Compare Danish Jakob, Swedish Jakob, Icelandic Jakob, Faroese Jákup and Czech Jakub (“male given names”).

1004696.etyen:
One of several Norwegian spellings of a female given name going back to Latin Otilia, originally Odilia, a Latinised form of Old High German Odila and Otila, pet forms of names such as Oda. The Old High German names are formed from the Germanic name element reflected in *audaz (“wealth, riches”), with a pet-name or diminutive ending.
Compare Danish Otelie, Swedish Otelie, German Ottilie and English Ottilie (“female given name”).
